title: From Arc to Dia: Lessons learned building AI Browsers – Samir Mody, The Browser Company of New York

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's most distinctive technical contribution is framing browsers as facing a lethal trifecta for prompt injection and detailing blended technical and UX mitigation strategies. Dia is an AI-native consumer browser targeting individual productivity and browsing. The talk covers shipping Dia in production and operating it with security mitigations like user confirmation steps. Content blends accessible product lessons with intermediate security and prompt engineering concepts. This is a conference talk from the AI Engineer channel.

summary: Samir Mody, Head of AI Engineering at The Browser Company, recounts the journey from Arc (2022) to Dia (2025), an AI-native browser. Founded in 2019, the company shipped Arc to millions but felt it didn't fully realize their vision. Access to GPT-class LLMs in 2022 sparked prototyping, leading to their Act 2 thesis in early 2024 that AI transforms browsing. Mody shares several major lessons. First, optimizing tools and process: the company moved from a rudimentary dev-only prompt editor to embedding all tools—prompts, context, models, parameters—directly into the internal product, enabling company-wide access and 10x'ing iteration speed. Second, Jeba is a sample-efficient prompt optimization mechanism that seeds prompts, executes tasks, scores them, uses PA selection, and leverages an LLM to reflect and mutate prompts iteratively, avoiding RL or fine-tuning. Product development follows phases: broad ideation with dogfooding, then eval-driven refinement and hill climbing before shipping. Third, model behavior is treated as a dedicated craft spanning behavior design, data collection, and model steering. The team was catalyzed when a strategy and ops member rewrote all prompts over a weekend, showing the best practitioners may not be engineers. Fourth, AI security is an emergent property of product building. Browsers face a lethal trifecta: access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and ability to externally communicate. Technical strategies like wrapping untrusted content in tags or separating data from instructions via system/user roles help but offer no guarantees against prompt injections. The company blends technical and UX approaches—exemplified by Dia's autofill tool, which requires user confirmation in plain text before writing to forms. Similar confirmation steps exist for scheduling events and writing emails. Mody closes by emphasizing the transition was not just product evolution but company evolution—affecting how they train, hire, communicate, and collaborate—and urges embracing technology shifts with conviction.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: The Browser Company transitioned from Arc (2022) to Dia (2025), an AI-native browser, driven by their Act 2 thesis that AI transforms browsing.
Embedding all AI tools—prompts, context, models, parameters—directly into the internal product 10x'd iteration speed and widened access beyond engineers to the whole company.
Jeba is a sample-efficient prompt optimization mechanism using PA selection and reflective prompt mutation, avoiding RL or fine-tuning.
Product development follows two phases: broad ideation with low barriers and dogfooding, then eval-driven refinement and hill climbing before shipping.
Model behavior is treated as a dedicated craft spanning behavior design, data collection, and model steering; the best practitioners may not be engineers.
Browsers face a lethal trifecta for prompt injection: access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and ability to externally communicate.
Technical strategies alone (tag wrapping, role separation) cannot guarantee prompt injection prevention; security requires blending technology, UX, and design from the ground up.
Dia's autofill tool mitigates prompt injection risk via user confirmation in plain text before writing to forms; similar confirmation steps exist for scheduling and email features.
The Arc-to-Dia transition was a company evolution, not just a product one, affecting training, hiring, communication, and collaboration.
When recognizing a technology shift, embrace it with conviction.

sections.title: Introduction and The Browser Company Background
sections.summary: Samir Mody introduces himself and The Browser Company, founded in 2019 with a mission to rethink browser usage. Arc shipped in 2022 as an incremental improvement but didn't fully hit the vision. Access to GPT models in 2022 began prototyping, leading to the Act 2 thesis in early 2024 that AI transforms browsing. Dia, an AI-native browser, shipped in early 2025.

sections.title: Optimizing Tools and Process for Faster Iteration
sections.summary: The company invests in tooling across prototyping, evals, data collection, and automation for hill climbing. They moved from a rudimentary dev-only prompt editor to embedding all tools—prompts, context, models, parameters—into the internal product, enabling company-wide access and 10x'ing iteration speed. This applied to memory knowledge graph and computer use mechanisms as well.

sections.title: Jeba: Prompt Optimization and Hill Climbing
sections.summary: Mody explains Jeba, a sample-efficient mechanism to improve complex LLM systems without RL or fine-tuning. It seeds prompts, executes tasks, scores them, uses PA selection to pick the best, then uses an LLM to reflect and generate new prompts. Key innovations are reflective prompt mutation, exploratory selection, and tuning text not weights.

sections.title: Product Development Phases: Ideation and Refinement
sections.summary: Features are built in phases: prototyping and ideation with broad participation and dogfooding, then eval collection and refinement through code, prompting, and automation like Jeba before shipping. Both phases are critical given weekly AI advancements unlocking new possibilities in Dia.

sections.title: Model Behavior as a Craft and Discipline
sections.summary: Model behavior defines, evaluates, and ships desired model behavior—turning principles into requirements, prompts, and evals. It covers behavior design, data collection, and model steering. Mody analogizes it to internet product design's evolution from functional to complex. The model behavior team was catalyzed by a strategy and ops member who rewrote prompts over a weekend, showing non-engineers can excel at model steering.

sections.title: AI Security: Prompt Injections and the Lethal Trifecta
sections.summary: Mody defines prompt injection as a third party overriding LLM instructions to cause harm—data exfiltration, malicious commands, or ignoring safety rules. Browsers are especially vulnerable due to a lethal trifecta: access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and ability to externally communicate. Technical strategies like wrapping untrusted content in tags or separating data and instructions via system/user roles with randomly generated tags help but offer no guarantees. The company blends technology, UX, and design to solve this from the ground up, exemplified by Dia's autofill tool requiring user confirmation in plain text before writing to forms, with similar confirmation steps for scheduling events and writing emails.

sections.title: Closing: Embracing the Technology Shift with Conviction
sections.summary: Mody recaps three lessons—optimizing tools and process, model behavior as craft, and AI security as emergent property—and reflects that the Arc-to-Dia journey was not just product evolution but company evolution. It changed how they train, hire, communicate, and collaborate. He urges the audience to recognize technology shifts and embrace them with conviction.

demonstrations: Jeba shown optimizing a simple prompt along metrics and scoring mechanisms the team created.
Prompt injection example: website HTML contains hidden injection causing LLM to exfiltrate personal data via GET parameters instead of summarizing.
Dia autofill tool: user confirmation in plain text before form data is written, giving user control and awareness.
limitations: Dia has not yet achieved the company's full vision but is believed to be on the way.
Initial rudimentary prompt editor had limited access (engineers only), slow iteration, and no personal context.
Arc was only an incremental improvement and didn't hit the company's original vision.
Technical strategies against prompt injection (tag wrapping, role separation) offer no guarantees; prompt injections will still happen.
